- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
**The Laundromat at 3 a.m.**

The Suds & Duds never closes, which is why Marisol goes there when sleep won't come. The fluorescent lights hum a note somewhere between B and B-flat. She has checked, using an app on her phone, in the way of people who need their insomnia to produce something.

Tonight she has a single load: two work shirts, a towel, and the gray sweater she has been meaning to wash since March. She feeds quarters into Machine 6 and sits on the orange plastic chair that has always been slightly too low, as though the room wants you humbled.

There is one other person there, an old man at the folding table, working through a mountain of children's clothes. Tiny socks. A dinosaur pajama top. A dress with sunflowers stitched along the hem. He folds each piece with terrible care, smoothing it flat with the side of his hand before making the creases.

She tries not to watch. Then she watches.

"Grandkids," he says without looking up. It isn't quite a question he's answering. It's more that he has learned people wonder.

"That's a lot of grandkids."

"Three. But they go through it. You would not believe." He holds up the dinosaur top. "This one, the boy, he's four. He believes he's allowed to be a different animal every day, and he's been right so far. Monday a tiger. Tuesday, this." He shakes the dinosaur gently. "Wednesday he was a fire truck. I don't know how to fold a fire truck."

Marisol laughs, and it surprises her. It comes out rusty, like a gate.

The machine sloshes and turns. Through its round window her shirts go under and rise, under and rise, like swimmers who keep changing their minds.

"My daughter works nights," the old man continues. "Hospital. So I come here, the kids are asleep at her place, my wife is asleep at ours, and I do the laundry. Nobody asked me to. It's just that the hours are the same as mine. When you get to be my age, sleep stops being a country you live in. It's more a place you visit, and the visas keep getting denied."

"I know the feeling," Marisol says. "Not the age. The visa."

"How old are you?"

"Thirty-four."

He nods slowly, as if this were a reasonable answer to a more important question. "That's a good age for the visa to be denied. You still have time to appeal."

She smiles at the linoleum. Between her shoes the floor has a faint brown stain shaped like Australia, or maybe Ohio.

For a while neither of them speaks. The dryers thump. Somewhere outside a bus sighs at a stop and moves on without anyone getting off. Marisol thinks about how many of these rooms exist, how many small bright boxes across the city are holding one or two awake people at this hour, all of them pretending to be here for the laundry. It comforts her, this secret population. A whole civilization of the sleepless, tending their socks.

"Can I tell you something stupid?" she says.

"Please. It's the only kind of thing anyone says after midnight."

"I've been in this city six years and I don't think I've had a real conversation with a stranger in about five and a half of them."

"That's not stupid. That's a statistic."

"It feels stupid. Like I should have done something about it."

He finishes a fold, sets the sunflower dress on the pile, and finally looks at her. His eyes are pale, the blue that has been washed many times itself. "What would you have done?"

"I don't know. Joined something. A choir. A hiking group."

"Do you like hiking?"

"No."

"Do you sing?"

"Badly."

"Then it's good you didn't. A bad choir is a terrible thing to be trapped in." He picks up a sock the size of his thumb, frowns, and hunts through the pile for its twin. "My experience is that nobody joins their way out of loneliness. It's more that one night you're in a laundromat and a man says something about a fire truck, and you answer, and that's the whole trick. It's not even a trick. It's just two people, a small mistake in the schedule of the universe."

"A mistake?"

"Sure. You were supposed to be asleep. So was I. Look what happens when the system fails."

Machine 6 shudders into its spin cycle and the whole row of machines seems to lean toward it. Marisol feels something in her chest loosen by a quarter turn, the way a jar lid does when you've stopped trying so hard.

"What's your name?" she asks.

"Anselm. Terrible name, my mother's idea. She was reading something."

"Marisol."

"Now that is a good name. It means sea and sun, doesn't it? Two things that don't sleep either."

"I think it's *sea and sun*, yes. I never thought about the sleeping part."

"Well. Now you've got something to think about at three in the morning besides your regrets."

She wants to say she doesn't have that many regrets, but it wouldn't be true, and the room is not a place for small lies. Instead she says, "Do you want help? With the folding?"

He considers her offer with the gravity of a man reviewing a treaty. "Do you know how to fold a fire truck?"

"No."

"Excellent. Neither do I. We'll figure it out together."

She crosses the room and he pushes half the pile toward her. The clothes are warm from the dryer, and they smell like every clean thing: cut grass, cotton, the inside of a cupboard in a house where people are loved. She picks up a tiny pair of overalls and doesn't know what to do with them, and he shows her: legs in, then thirds, sleeves tucked like folded wings.

Behind them Machine 6 winds down, ticking as it slows. Her shirts will be wet and heavy and ready to move on. But not yet. There's a sweater in there that has waited since March, and it can wait a few minutes longer while she learns to fold the sleeve of a dinosaur.

Outside, the sky begins its slow argument with the dark. Neither of them notices. They are busy, in the good way, the way people are when their hands have been given something small and necessary to do.

"Not bad," Anselm says, inspecting her work. "You have a gift."

"For overalls?"

"For showing up at the wrong hour," he says, "and staying."
---

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. This is a crafted short story whose quiet, midnight encounter turns insomnia and loneliness toward tentative companionship.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm, observant, and gently comic, finding emotional weight in small details: a fluorescent hum, a sunflower dress, a tiny sock. Marisol’s sleeplessness and regret are met not with a grand solution but with conversation and shared work. The story invites the reader to see ordinary, accidental contact as meaningful without pretending it cures loneliness; its closing image of learning to fold a dinosaur’s sleeve keeps that hope modest and tactile.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds insomnia, urban isolation, intergenerational contact, and the consolations of practical care. Laundry, children’s clothes, and the late-night laundromat become a setting where people who feel out of step with ordinary schedules can recognize one another. Its moral emphasis is that connection may begin through showing up and staying, rather than through a planned effort to escape loneliness.

## Evidence line
> My experience is that nobody joins their way out of loneliness.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story’s recurring attention to humble objects and its consistent, unsentimental tenderness make those choices especially legible here.
